places: Traditional birthplace of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha; birth c. 563 or c. 480 BCE (debated). Ashoka's pillar of c. 249 BCE marks the spot
Capital of the Shakya clan where the young Gautama grew up; whether it was at Tilaurakot (Nepal) or Piprahwa (India) is debated
Gautama reaches awakening under the Bodhi tree; c. 528 BCE in the traditional chronology, c. 450 BCE or later in the short chronology (debated)
First sermon in the deer park; later a great monastery with Ashoka's lion capital. Sacked by Muslim armies c. 1194 (date approximate)
Jetavana monastery, donated by the merchant Anathapindika; the Buddha spent many rainy seasons here
Capital of Magadha; by tradition the First Council recites the Buddha's teachings here soon after his death (historicity debated)

Ashoka's bloody conquest of Kalinga; his 13th Rock Edict records his remorse and turn to the dharma
Ashoka's capital; Theravada chronicles place a Third Council here under Moggaliputta-Tissa and say it sent missionaries abroad (known only from that tradition)

Ashoka's mission of Sona and Uttara to the 'Golden Land'; its location (Lower Burma, Thailand or elsewhere) is debated

Great stupa of the Andhra region, enlarged from the 3rd century BCE to the 3rd century CE
Stupa railings carved c. 150 BCE: early Buddhist art showing the Buddha only by symbols
Rock-cut monasteries; first phase c. 2nd century BCE, famous murals of the second phase c. 460-480 CE
Capital of the Indo-Greek king Menander I, remembered as 'Milinda' in a Buddhist dialogue
Rock-cut prayer hall paid for by merchants, some of them Yavanas (Greeks); site developed from the 2nd century BCE
Monks write down the Pali Canon on palm leaves for the first time, c. 29 BCE (date varies by source)
Earliest secure Chinese record of Buddhist practice: Prince Ying of Chu honours the Buddha (65 CE)
By legend Emperor Ming's dream brings two Indian monks and sutras on white horses; China's first Buddhist temple (traditional date)
Kushan-era workshops carve some of the first images of the Buddha in human form (whether before Gandhara is debated)
Gandharan monasteries with stucco sculpture, 1st-7th centuries; end date approximate
Kushan cave monasteries on the Amu Darya; Buddhism fades after the Arab conquest (approximate)
Buddhist oasis kingdom (arrival date uncertain); Faxian sees its image processions in 401. Conquered by the Muslim Karakhanids in 1006
Kushan emperor Kanishka (r. c. 127-150) builds one of the tallest stupas of the ancient world
The Parthian prince-monk An Shigao begins translating Buddhist texts into Chinese
'New Monastery' near Balkh, perhaps founded in Kanishka's time; flourishing in the 7th-11th centuries by historical accounts
Stupas with Roman-influenced wall paintings in the kingdom of Shanshan (Kroraina); abandoned in the late 1st millennium
Tocharian Buddhist kingdom, birthplace of Kumarajiva (344); Islamised in the 14th-15th centuries (approximate)
Early centre of Buddhism in Jiaozhi on the sea route from India, 2nd-3rd centuries (approximate)
Monasteries of the Ikshvaku kings' capital in the 3rd century CE; the link with the philosopher Nagarjuna is debated
More than 230 painted cave shrines of the Kucha kingdom, 3rd-8th centuries (dating debated)
The monk Lezun digs the first meditation cave; nearly 500 painted caves follow over a thousand years
The monk Sundo brings images and sutras from the Former Qin; Buddhism adopted at court
The Serindian monk Marananta arrives from Eastern Jin China
Huiyuan founds Donglin Temple, later revered as the starting point of Pure Land Buddhism
Buddhist oasis kingdom visited by Xuanzang in 630; from 843 the Uyghur kingdom of Qocho, Buddhist until Islamisation in the 15th century (approximate)
Kumarajiva arrives under Later Qin patronage; his translation bureau shapes Chinese Buddhism until his death in 413
Great monastic university founded under the Guptas c. 427; sacked by Bakhtiyar Khalji c. 1193 (date debated), afterwards continued only in reduced form
Stupa traditionally dated to the 5th century; Newar Buddhism of the valley later preserves Sanskrit texts and tantric rites
Northern Wei emperors carve colossal Buddhas near their capital Pingcheng
After moving the capital to Luoyang the Northern Wei start the Longmen caves; work continues into the Tang
Founded for an Indian monk; later legend links it with Bodhidharma, founder of Chan (Zen)
Largest Pyu city; Pali inscriptions and stupas show Theravada (with Mahayana) from about the 5th century
After the martyrdom of the courtier Ichadon, King Beopheung makes Buddhism Silla's official faith
Baekje sends a Buddha image and sutras to the Japanese court in 538 or 552 (the sources differ)

Temple traditionally founded by Prince Shotoku
Japan's first full temple, built by the Soga clan from 588
Cave temples above Turfan with Uyghur-era murals of donors and Buddhas (5th-14th centuries)
Mon Buddhist polities of central Thailand, 6th-11th centuries
Founded by Prince Shotoku; its rebuilt halls are among the oldest wooden buildings in the world
Buddhist caves (c. 600-730) beside Hindu and Jain ones: Buddhism as one faith among several
King Songtsen Gampo builds the Jokhang for a Buddha image brought by his Nepali queen (her historicity is debated)
Emperor Harsha holds a great religious assembly honouring the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang
Brick temple-monastery complex on the Batang Hari river, 7th-13th centuries
Pagoda built to house the texts Xuanzang brought back from India
Yijing finds over a thousand monks here in 671; Srivijaya's power fades in the 13th century (approximate)
Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch, teaches here; his 'sudden awakening' school becomes mainstream Chan
Pala monastic university founded in the 8th century; destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khalji's troops c. 1193 (date debated)
Emperor Shomu's Great Buddha, a bronze about 15 m tall, is dedicated
Temple founded by the blind Chinese master Jianzhen (Ganjin), who brought proper ordination rules
Silla's great temple and cave shrine; work begun in 751 is completed in 774
First Tibetan monastery, founded under Trisong Detsen by Shantarakshita and Padmasambhava; first monks ordained in 779
Saicho founds the Tendai school's headquarters, cradle of later Japanese schools
Monastic university founded by the Pala king Dharmapala (r. 783-820); destroyed c. 1203
Sailendra kings build the largest Buddhist monument, with 2,672 relief panels and 504 Buddhas; Java turns Muslim in the 15th-16th centuries
Kukai founds the centre of Shingon esoteric Buddhism
Assassination of Langdarma ends the Tibetan Empire; monastic Buddhism in central Tibet declines for over a century
Emperor Wuzong closes some 4,600 monasteries and returns monks and nuns to lay life; Chinese Buddhism never regains its Tang wealth
The Diamond Sutra, the oldest dated printed book (11 May 868), later sealed in the 'Library Cave' c. 1000 and found in 1900
The whole Buddhist canon is printed from woodblocks, 971-983
Tangut state patronises Buddhism and prints the canon in its own script; destroyed by the Mongols in 1227
The Bengali master Atisha arrives in western Tibet, starting the 'later spread' of Buddhism
Ly dynasty royal pagoda; Buddhism at the height of court patronage
Liao (Khitan) dynasty builds the world's tallest surviving wooden pagoda
By the chronicles King Anawrahta takes Thaton in 1057 and adopts Theravada (debated); over 10,000 temples built in 250 years
Sakya monastery founded; its lamas later rule Tibet for the Mongols
Temples with Kashmiri-style murals; dated 11th century by tradition, no earlier than c. 1140 by recent readings (debated)
Parakramabahu I unites Sri Lanka's monastic orders under the Mahavihara tradition
Honen founds the Jodo (Pure Land) school: salvation by reciting Amida's name
Jayavarman VII (r. 1181-c. 1218) makes Mahayana the state faith and builds the Bayon
Dogen founds the head temple of Soto Zen
About 81,000 woodblocks of the canon, carved 1237-1251 to invoke protection against the Mongols, later kept at Haeinsa
Bronze Amida Buddha cast for the warrior capital
Hulagu's Mongol rulers of Iran patronise Buddhist temples; Ghazan's conversion to Islam in 1295 ends it
Kublai Khan makes the Sakya lama Phagpa his national preceptor; Tibetan Buddhism at the Yuan court
Ram Khamhaeng's inscription (1292; authenticity debated) praises Lankan-lineage monks
The retired emperor Tran Nhan Tong founds the Vietnamese Truc Lam Zen school
Within about a century of Jayavarman VII the Khmer turn to Theravada; Angkor Wat becomes a Buddhist shrine (approximate)
Court blends Shiva worship and tantric Buddhism; decline of the kingdom by 1527 (approximate)
Thai kingdom with Theravada as court religion until its sack by the Burmese in 1767; Buddhism continues under Bangkok
Fa Ngum founds Lan Xang with Khmer support; the Phra Bang image becomes the palladium of Laos
Tsongkhapa founds the first Gelug ('Yellow Hat') monastery
King Tilokarat of Lan Na hosts a council to revise the Pali Canon (numbered the eighth in Thai tradition)
Altan Khan meets Sonam Gyatso and gives him the title Dalai Lama; the Mongols turn to Tibetan Buddhism
Altan Khan's city gets its first great Tibetan Buddhist temple
Abtai Khan builds the first major monastery of the Khalkha Mongols from the ruins of Karakorum
The Buddha's tooth relic, symbol of kingship, is housed in the last Sinhalese royal capital
Oirat Mongols migrate to the lower Volga and found the Kalmyk Khanate: Europe's only traditionally Buddhist people
Ngawang Namgyal unifies Bhutan as a Drukpa Kagyu Buddhist state in the 1630s
A mobile monastery-camp founded for Zanabazar, first Jebtsundamba Khutuktu; it grows into Mongolia's capital
Three lamas consecrate Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Buddhist king of Sikkim
The 5th Dalai Lama, now ruler of Tibet, begins the Potala Palace
Russia formally recognises the Buddhism of the Buryats; datsans (monastic colleges) multiply
Qing emperor Qianlong turns a palace into a Tibetan Buddhist monastery
Monks from Ayutthaya under Upali Thera restore full ordination in Sri Lanka
King Mindon's council has the Pali Canon carved on 729 marble slabs at the Kuthodaw Pagoda
Founded by Blavatsky and Olcott; it popularises Asian religions in the West
Edwin Arnold's verse life of the Buddha becomes a bestseller in Britain and America
Theosophists Henry Olcott and Helena Blavatsky formally take the Buddhist precepts; Olcott later backs Buddhist schools
Jodo Shinshu priests follow Japanese plantation workers to Hawaii (approximate)
Anagarika Dharmapala founds the society to return Bodh Gaya to Buddhist care
Anagarika Dharmapala and the Zen abbot Soyen Shaku present Buddhism at the World's Parliament of Religions
Japanese immigrants found the Buddhist Mission of North America, later the Buddhist Churches of America
Muhammad begins preaching after his first revelation in the cave of Hira (traditionally 610); persecuted, his followers leave in 622
Muhammad and his followers emigrate from Mecca (the Hijra, September 622, year 1 of the Islamic calendar); Medina becomes the first Muslim community-state
Mecca opens its gates to Muslim forces almost without fighting (January 630); the idols of the Kaaba are destroyed
Badhan, the Persian governor of Yemen, accepts Islam (c. 628); Yemeni tribes join in the 'Year of Delegations' (630-631)
The Julanda rulers of Oman accept Islam (c. 630); Oman later becomes the heartland of Ibadi Islam
Arab armies take Damascus (634, again 636); Umayyad capital from 661. Christians remained the majority of Syria for centuries
Caliph al-Walid I builds the Great Mosque of Damascus (705-715) on the site of the church of St John the Baptist
Jerusalem surrenders to Caliph Umar after a siege (637 or 638; dates vary)
Caliph Abd al-Malik completes the Dome of the Rock (691-692), the oldest surviving major Islamic monument
Founded as an Arab garrison town (c. 636-638); later a centre of Arabic grammar and theology
Founded as a garrison town (638); Ali's capital (656-661) and an early centre of Shia Islam
Husayn, grandson of Muhammad, is killed by Umayyad troops (10 October 680); his martyrdom becomes central to Shia Islam
Amr ibn al-As takes the Byzantine fortress of Babylon (April 641); Egypt's Coptic Christians remained the majority for centuries (when Muslims became the majority is debated)
Founded as the Arab garrison capital of Egypt (641-642), around the Mosque of Amr ibn al-As
Caliph al-Mansur founds the Round City of Baghdad (30 July 762), the Abbasid capital
Abbasid library and translation centre: Greek, Persian and Indian works are translated into Arabic (flourished c. 830s)
The Ismaili Fatimids conquer Egypt and found Cairo (969); al-Azhar mosque 970-972
Al-Hadi ila'l-Haqq Yahya founds the Zaydi imamate in northern Yemen (897), which lasted until 1962
Taken after the battle of Nahavand (c. 642-643); most Iranians converted only over the next two to three centuries (Bulliet; debated)
Surrenders in 651; its biographical dictionaries are the main source for Richard Bulliet's conversion curve (Iran majority Muslim c. 9th-10th century, debated)
The last Sasanian king Yazdegerd III is killed near Merv (651); base for Arab conquests in Central Asia
Qutayba ibn Muslim takes Bukhara (709) and builds a mosque in the citadel; capital of the Persian Samanids (819-999)
Qutayba ibn Muslim takes Samarkand (712); later famous for paper-making
Kabul resisted Arab armies for two centuries; the Saffarid Ya'qub ibn al-Layth takes it (c. 870)
Satuq Bughra Khan, first Muslim ruler of the Turkic Kara-Khanids, converts (c. 934; date debated)
Ibn al-Athir records that '200,000 tents of Turks' converted in 960; the Kara-Khanid realm becomes Muslim
The Kara-Khanids conquer the Buddhist kingdom of Khotan after a long war (c. 1006)
The Sufi Khoja Ahmed Yasawi (d. 1166) preaches among the steppe Turks; Timur builds his mausoleum (1389-1405)
Ibn Fadlan arrives with an Abbasid embassy (May 922); the Volga Bulgar ruler Almış adopts Islam as state religion
Özbeg Khan makes Islam the religion of the Golden Horde (1313); Berke (r. 1257-1266) had been the first Muslim khan
Özbeg's mosque at Solkhat (Staryi Krym) is built (1314); the Crimean Khanate (1441-1783) remains Muslim
The Kazan Khanate is founded (c. 1438); Russia conquers it in 1552 and destroys its mosques, but the Volga Tatars remain Muslim
Tarmashirin, Chagatai khan, converts (c. 1326); Ibn Battuta visits his camp
Buddhist Turpan becomes Muslim under the Moghul (Chagatai) khans during the 15th century
Arab frontier fortress against the Khazars; Juma Mosque founded 734; Dagestan converts gradually over centuries
Sheikh Mansur calls the Chechens to Islam and resistance against Russia (1785); Islam had spread there gradually in the 16th-18th centuries
Seljuk Turks take Konya (c. 1084), later capital of the Sultanate of Rum; the Sufi poet Rumi dies here (1273)
Ottomans take Bursa (1326), their first capital
Ottomans take Adrianople/Edirne (1360s; date debated) and make it their capital
After the fall of Constantinople (29 May 1453) Hagia Sophia becomes a mosque
Ottomans conquer Bosnia (1463); much of the population converts over the 1500s-1600s (speed and causes debated)
Skanderbeg's fortress falls (1478); most Albanians convert in the 1600s-1700s
Ottomans take Buda (August 1541); its Muslim population is killed or expelled when the Habsburgs retake it (September 1686)
Andalusi exiles conquer Crete and found Chandax (c. 824-827); Byzantines retake it (March 961)
Tariq ibn Ziyad lands with Berber and Arab troops (April 711); the rock is named after him (Jabal Tariq)
Taken in 711; capital of al-Andalus, a caliphate from 929; Castile takes it in June 1236
Abd al-Rahman I begins the Great Mosque (785); it became a cathedral after 1236
The Visigothic capital falls (711-712); Alfonso VI of Castile takes it (May 1085)
Taken 712-713; Almohad capital in al-Andalus; Castile takes it (November 1248)
Taken c. 714; Portuguese and crusaders take it (October 1147)
Taken c. 714; Aragon takes it (1238), but Muslim peasants (later Moriscos) remain numerous in the countryside until 1609
Last Muslim state in Iberia (Nasrid emirate 1238-1492) surrenders on 2 January 1492; Muslims forced to convert from 1501-1502

Arab-Berber forces take Narbonne (c. 719); the Franks retake it (759)

Musa ibn Nusayr takes Tangier (c. 708); many Berbers convert and join the armies, but unequal treatment leads to the Berber Revolt (740)
Founded 757 by Sufri Kharijite Berbers; northern port of the trans-Saharan gold trade
Capital of the Ibadi Rustamid imamate (c. 777-909), linked to trans-Saharan trade
Idris I founds Fez (789); al-Qarawiyyin mosque-university founded 859
The Ismaili Fatimids found Mahdia as their capital (916-921)
The Almoravids, a Sanhaja Berber reform movement, found Marrakesh (c. 1070)
Al-Bakri (1068) describes Ghana's capital with a separate Muslim merchants' town of 12 mosques; whether the Almoravids conquered Ghana (1076) is debated
Al-Sadi's chronicle names Zuwa Kusoy (1009-1010) as the first ruler of Gao to convert
King War Jabi (d. 1040/41) makes Takrur on the Senegal River one of the first Muslim states of West Africa

Capital of Mali (location debated); Mansa Musa leaves for Mecca (1324)
Founded by Tuareg c. 1100; under Mali and Songhai a centre of scholarship with its Sankore, Sidi Yahya and Djinguereber mosques

Islamic centre of the Hausa states; the Gobarau minaret dates from the 15th-16th century

Capital of the Sokoto Caliphate (founded 1809), one of Africa's largest 19th-century states
Seku Amadu leads a jihad (1818) and founds the Massina Caliphate with its capital Hamdullahi
A Fulani jihad founds the Imamate of Futa Jallon (c. 1725)
The Torodbe revolution creates the Imamate of Futa Toro (1776)
Malê revolt: enslaved African Muslims rise in Salvador (January 1835)
Early Muslims persecuted in Mecca find refuge with the Christian king (Najashi) of Aksum (c. 615)
Its Masjid al-Qiblatayn is traditionally dated to the 7th century (debated); Zeila later becomes a port of the Adal Sultanate
Muslim trading community of the 8th century; Mark Horton dates the first excavated timber mosque to c. 780, the earliest evidence of Islam on the Swahili coast
Muslim trading town of the Somali coast; the Fakr ad-Din and Arba'a Rukun mosques date from 1268-1269
Swahili city-state (sultanate from c. 10th century); its Great Mosque begun in the 11th century; Ibn Battuta visits in 1331

The Auwal Mosque, South Africa's first (1794), serves Muslims brought from Southeast Asia as exiles and slaves

Ghaznavids take Lahore (c. 1021); the Sufi Ali Hujwiri (Data Ganj Bakhsh) settles there (11th century)

Bakhtiyar Khalji takes Nadia and Lakhnauti (c. 1204-1205), beginning Muslim rule in Bengal
The Sufi Shah Jalal arrives with the conquest of Sylhet (1303)
Khan Jahan Ali clears the Sundarbans fringe and builds the Sixty Dome Mosque (15th century)
Mughal capital of Bengal (1610); Eaton argues eastern Bengal's peasants became Muslim as forests were cleared for rice under Mughal rule (16th-18th c.; debated)

Akbar builds his new capital (1571-1585) beside the shrine of the Sufi Salim Chishti
Arab traders settle on Sri Lanka's west coast; tradition makes Beruwala the first Muslim settlement (date debated)
King Dhovemi converts (1153) and the Maldives become Muslim

Muslim gravestones from 1368 onward at the Hindu-Buddhist Majapahit capital show Muslims at court
Tomb of Malik Ibrahim (d. 1419), first of the Wali Sanga, the 'nine saints' of Javanese tradition

Raden Patah founds Demak, Java's first Muslim sultanate (c. 1475); Great Mosque c. 1479
The Aceh Sultanate is founded (c. 1496), later called 'Mecca's veranda'
The king of Patani converts (traditionally 1457; debated)
Brunei's ruler Muhammad Shah converts (traditionally 1368; some historians date it c. 1515)
Makhdum Karim brings Islam to Sulu (c. 1380, traditional); the Sultanate of Sulu is founded in the 15th century (1405 or 1457)

The Muslim kingdom of Maynila (Rajah Sulayman) is linked to Brunei; Spain takes it (1571) and Catholicism replaces Islam
Ternate's royal family converts under Marhum (r. 1465-1486); his son Zainal Abidin makes it a sultanate (1486)

Padri reformists back from Mecca start a war with Minangkabau traditional leaders (1803-1837) that draws in the Dutch
Arab and Persian merchants live in Guangzhou by the 8th century; tradition dates the Huaisheng Mosque to 627 (likely later)

Niujie Mosque, traditionally founded 996, Beijing's oldest mosque

Safavid conversion of Iran to Shia Islam

Afghan cameleers build the Adelaide Mosque (1888-1889), Australia's oldest surviving city mosque
The Shah Jahan Mosque, first purpose-built mosque in Britain (1889)
Omar ibn Said, an enslaved West African scholar, writes his autobiography in Arabic (1831)
Portugal captures Ceuta on 21 August 1415, the first European overseas conquest of the age of expansion; Prince Henry takes part.

A Portuguese trading post on Arguin island (from 1445, fort c. 1448) buys gold and captives from Saharan traders.

Settled from 1493, São Tomé becomes the model of the plantation island: sugar grown by enslaved Africans for export.
Afonso de Albuquerque takes Goa on 25 November 1510; it becomes the capital of Portuguese Asia and an entry point for American plants such as chili.
Portugal captures Malacca in August 1511, gaining the strait between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea.
After a failed attempt in 1507, Portugal takes Hormuz, gateway to the Persian Gulf, in 1515 and holds it as a client state until 1622.
Portuguese merchants settle at Macau around 1557 with Ming permission; it links China with Nagasaki, Malacca and Goa.
The port opens to Portuguese ships in 1571; Japanese silver and Chinese silk pass through it until the Portuguese are expelled in 1639.
Founded in 1576, Luanda becomes the main port of the Angolan slave trade to Brazil.
The Dutch East India Company founds Batavia (Jakarta) in 1619 as its Asian headquarters.
From 1503 the House of Trade in Seville controls Spanish shipping and silver from the Americas.
On 7 June 1494 Spain and Portugal divide the newly found lands along a meridian 370 leagues west of Cape Verde.
Columbus's second voyage (17 ships, over 1,000 men) founds the first Spanish town in January 1494 and lands horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, goats and sugarcane.
Founded by Bartholomew Columbus in 1496, the oldest continuously inhabited European city in the Americas.
By around 1516 the first sugar mills on Hispaniola grind cane brought by Columbus in 1493; enslaved Africans replace a dying Taíno workforce.
Havana moves to its present harbour in 1519 and becomes the gathering port of the Spanish treasure fleets.

Juan Garrido, an African-born conquistador, is credited with the first wheat harvest in New Spain (early 1520s).

Founded on 1 June 1533; a fortified treasure-fleet port and one of the main slave markets of Spanish America.

Pizarro founds Lima on 18 January 1535; it becomes the capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru.

Silver is found at the Cerro Rico in 1545; worked largely by Indigenous mita labour, it yields an estimated 60% of the world's silver in the late 16th century and the town grows past 200,000 people (estimate).
Silver is discovered at Zacatecas in 1546, the start of northern Mexico's silver boom.
The Santa Bárbara mercury mine (from the 1560s) supplies mercury for amalgamating Potosí silver; mita workers suffer mercury poisoning.
Urdaneta reaches Acapulco on 8 October 1565, opening the return route from Asia; galleons sail between Acapulco and Manila until 1815.
In 1567 the Ming allow private overseas trade from Yuegang (Haicheng), Fujian; much American silver enters China here via Manila.
Legazpi founds Spanish Manila on 24 June 1571; American silver buys Chinese silk and porcelain brought by Fujianese merchants.
Pernambuco, founded in the 1530s, becomes the world's leading sugar region by c. 1600, worked by enslaved Africans.
Founded in 1549 as the capital of Portuguese Brazil and a main port of the slave trade.
Founded on 8 September 1565, the oldest continuously occupied European-founded settlement in the continental United States.
The first lasting English colony (14 May 1607), in the Powhatan paramount chiefdom; tobacco becomes its cash crop from 1612.
Champlain founds Quebec on 3 July 1608 as a fur-trading post allied with the Wendat and Innu.
Capital of New Mexico from 1610; in the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 the Pueblos drive out the Spanish and take their horses.
Settled in 1627; in the 1640s it turns to sugar and enslaved African labour, the 'sugar revolution' of the English Caribbean.
The first recorded syphilis epidemic in Europe breaks out among the armies at Naples in 1495; most evidence supports an American origin, but a pre-Columbian presence in Europe is debated.
The first recorded smallpox epidemic in the Americas strikes Hispaniola in December 1518, killing much of the surviving Taíno population.
Smallpox arrives from Hispaniola with Narváez's expedition in spring 1520 and spreads inland; tradition names an enslaved African man, Francisco de Eguía, as the first case.
Smallpox (huey zahuatl, 'great rash') ravages Tenochtitlan from autumn 1520 for about 70 days, killing the new ruler Cuitláhuac.
The Kaqchikel annals record a deadly plague around 1519–1521, before the Spanish reached the highlands; that it was smallpox is likely but debated.
An epidemic, often said to be smallpox (debated: measles or another fever), kills the ruler Huayna Capac and his heir c. 1527, opening a civil war between Huáscar and Atahualpa.
A measles epidemic, called 'small leprosy' in Nahuatl, sweeps central Mexico in 1531.
The great cocoliztli of 1545–48 kills an estimated 5–15 million in New Spain; ancient DNA from Teposcolula-Yucundaa points to Salmonella Paratyphi C, but the cause is debated.
Smallpox lands at La Serena with a ship in late 1561 and ravages Chile's native population into 1562.
Smallpox and other epidemics in the early 1560s kill large numbers of Indigenous people around Bahia, according to Jesuit reports.
Population history of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas
A second great cocoliztli (1576–80), after a severe drought, kills about 2 million; the physician Francisco Hernández describes it; the cause is debated.
An epidemic of 1616–1619 (cause debated) empties coastal villages such as Patuxet; the Pilgrims settle on its site in 1620.
Smallpox spreads through New England and the Connecticut valley in 1633–34.
Measles and smallpox in 1634–40 kill half to two-thirds of the Wendat, leaving about 12,000; Haudenosaunee attacks in 1649 destroy Wendake.
The first definite yellow fever epidemic in the Americas (1647), probably arriving with mosquitoes on slave ships from Africa; Yucatán follows in 1648.
Q'eqchi' Maya nobles bring chocolate to Prince Philip's court in 1544, the earliest documented chocolate in Europe; the first recorded cacao shipment follows in 1585.
Maize appears in Chinese local records from the mid-16th century (often dated c. 1555; approximate) and later spreads to hill land unsuited to rice.
Jean Nicot, French ambassador in Lisbon, sends tobacco and seeds to Paris in 1560 as a medicine; nicotine is named after him.
A receipt of 28 November 1567 for potatoes shipped from Gran Canaria to Antwerp is the first written record of potatoes outside the Americas.
Sweet potato is brought from Spanish Luzon to Fujian around 1594, after a major crop failure, and becomes a famine food.
Potatoes reach the British Isles between 1588 and 1593; Ireland is probably the first part of Europe to grow them widely, in the early 17th century.
The Portuguese bring chili peppers to Goa and other Asian ports in the 16th century (details unrecorded); in 1543 the German botanist Fuchs already calls one kind 'Calicut pepper'.
The encyclopedia Jibong yuseol (1614) is the first Korean mention of chili peppers, said to have come via Japan; they later transform kimchi and gochujang.
Portuguese traders bring cassava from Brazil to West-Central Africa in the 16th century; it slowly replaces sorghum and millet as a staple.
John Rolfe plants sweeter Caribbean tobacco in 1612; tobacco exports make the colony and drive demand for land and labour.
The first colonies of European honey bees are shipped from England to Virginia in 1622.
Louis XVI's finance minister Calonne asked hand-picked nobles and clergy to accept a land tax on everyone; they refused.
Townspeople threw roof tiles at royal troops sent to close the local parlement, an early open revolt against royal power.
Nobles, clergy and commoners of Dauphiné demanded an Estates-General with a doubled Third Estate voting by head.
A hailstorm swept across northern France and the Low Countries, flattening crops just before harvest; bread prices climbed through the harsh winter of 1788-89.
Workers sacked a wallpaper factory after rumours its owner wanted lower wages; troops fired and dozens to hundreds died (estimates vary).
The three estates met for the first time since 1614; the Third Estate refused to vote by order and on 17 June declared itself the National Assembly.
Locked out of their hall, the deputies swore in an indoor tennis court not to separate until France had a constitution.
A crowd seeking gunpowder took the royal fortress-prison, which held seven prisoners; about 98 attackers and several defenders died.
Rumours of brigands hired by nobles set off panic and attacks on châteaux; peasants burned manorial records of dues.
One of the starting points of the panic, which spread within days across Poitou and the south-west.
Peasants in the Mâconnais attacked dozens of châteaux and abbeys, burning title deeds.
The panic reached the Dauphiné, where châteaux were burned around Bourgoin.
Fear of brigands and of hoarders of grain spread through the grain lands north-east of Paris.
Abolition of feudalism (night of 4 August, Versailles)
In one night the Assembly voted to end feudal privileges, the church tithe and the sale of offices.
Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (Versailles)
Seventeen articles declared that men are born free and equal in rights and that sovereignty lies with the nation.

Thousands of women marched from Paris demanding bread; the next day the royal family was taken to the Tuileries in Paris.
Priests became elected state employees who had to swear an oath; about half refused, splitting the Church and the country.

The National Guard fired on a crowd petitioning for the king's removal; roughly a dozen to 50 died (estimates vary).
Thousands of émigré nobles and officers gathered around the king's brothers in Koblenz, hoping to restore the old order by force.
The Emperor and the King of Prussia declared support for Louis XVI, a vague threat that inflamed French opinion.
Enslaved people rose in the north of France's richest colony; within a week some 1,800 plantations were destroyed. It became the Haitian Revolution.

Insurgents stormed the palace and killed most of the Swiss Guards; the monarchy was suspended.

Charlotte Corday, a Girondin sympathiser from Caen, stabbed the radical journalist Jean-Paul Marat in his bath.

All unmarried men aged 18-25 were called up and the whole nation put on a war footing.

Robespierre led a state festival for a new civic religion of a Supreme Being, seven weeks before his fall.

French armies and Dutch Patriots replaced the Dutch Republic with a French sister republic.
The law of 18 Germinal Year III created the metre, gram and litre; the definitive platinum metre was deposited in the Archives on 22 June 1799.
A royalist rising in Paris was crushed with cannon fire organised by General Bonaparte.
Gracchus Babeuf's plot for a society of common property was betrayed; he was executed in 1797.
Bonaparte merged conquered Lombardy and neighbouring lands into a sister republic.
The old aristocratic Republic of Genoa became a French-style democratic republic.

French troops occupied Rome, exiled Pope Pius VI and set up a republic.

About 1,000 French troops under Humbert landed to support the Irish rebellion; they surrendered at Ballinamuck.
A short-lived republic in Naples, overthrown by a royalist peasant army; many of its leaders were executed.
French soldiers found the inscribed stone that later let Champollion decipher hieroglyphs (1822).

Back from Egypt, Bonaparte overthrew the Directory; when the Council of Five Hundred resisted, his brother Lucien called in the grenadiers. He became First Consul.
The central bank founded under the Consulate; with the franc germinal of 1803 it gave France a stable currency that lasted until 1914.

Metres and kilograms became France's only legal measures from 1801; resistance was such that Napoleon allowed the hybrid 'mesures usuelles' in 1812, and the pure system returned only in 1840. French rule carried it to the Low Countries and parts of Italy and Germany.

Leclerc's expedition of about 30,000 men tried to restore French control; Toussaint Louverture was deported, but yellow fever killed most of the army, including Leclerc (1 November 1802).
The only general peace in Europe between 1792 and 1814; it lasted just over a year.

The law of 20 May 1802 kept slavery in colonies where it had not been abolished, and it was forced back on Guadeloupe; Louis Delgrès and his followers blew themselves up at Matouba rather than surrender (28 May). France abolished slavery again only in 1848.
The leader of the Haitian Revolution, deported by Leclerc, died of illness and cold in a mountain prison in the Jura.

Dessalines proclaimed Haiti independent: the first state born of a successful slave revolt and the second independent state in the Americas.

The civil code: equality of men before the law, secure property, civil marriage and inheritance shared between sons - but wives were legally subordinate to husbands. It became the model for civil law in much of Europe, Latin America and the Middle East.

Beethoven's Third Symphony, first meant to honour Bonaparte; Beethoven withdrew the dedication after Napoleon made himself emperor (as his pupil Ries told it). First private performance June 1804, public premiere 7 April 1805.

16 German states, later almost 40, left the Holy Roman Empire under Napoleon's protection and supplied troops to his armies.

Francis II laid down the imperial crown, ending an empire that had lasted about a thousand years; he remained Emperor of Austria.

Jérôme Bonaparte's model kingdom: the first written constitution in Germany, the Code civil, legal equality for Jews - and heavy taxes and conscription.
Taken from Denmark in 1807, the small island became a depot from which British goods were smuggled into the Continent past Napoleon's customs.

The city held out in two sieges, fought street by street; in the second siege alone about 24,000 defenders and 30,000 civilians died, many of them of disease.

Partisan bands such as those of Espoz y Mina in Navarre and 'El Empecinado' in Castile ambushed convoys and couriers, tying down French troops across Spain; the word guerrilla ('little war') entered other languages from here.

The great survey of ancient and modern Egypt by the roughly 160 scholars who went with Bonaparte's expedition (1798–1801); the volumes appeared 1809–1829 and launched Egyptology and a craze for Egyptian style.
Tyrolean peasants under the innkeeper Andreas Hofer rose against Bavarian rule and took Innsbruck three times; Hofer was shot in Mantua in February 1810.
Austria's Adriatic lands were annexed to France after Wagram; French rule brought the Code civil, a centralised administration and new schools (with French as the official language).
With the Spanish king a prisoner of Napoleon, Caracas set up its own junta on 19 April 1810 and declared independence on 5 July 1811 - the start of the Spanish American wars of independence.
News that the Spanish central junta had fallen to the French led Buenos Aires to depose the viceroy and form its own government.
The priest Miguel Hidalgo called his parishioners to revolt, starting Mexico's war of independence.

Fires that raged from 14 to 18 September destroyed much of the largely wooden city after the French entered; the governor Rostopchin is often held responsible (debated).

A mass grave of Grande Armée soldiers was found in Vilnius in 2001; lice from it carried DNA of the bacteria of trench fever and typhus. Disease, above all typhus, killed far more men in 1812 than battle (proportions debated).
After the fall of Paris his marshals refused to fight on; Napoleon abdicated and on 20 April said farewell to the Old Guard in the Cour du Cheval-Blanc.
Painted in 1814, after the French left, to show the executions of 3 May 1808; with Goya's etchings 'The Disasters of War' it became one of the first great images of war's horror. Now in the Prado.
Napoleon ruled the island as a sovereign prince for ten months, building roads and reorganising its mines, before escaping to France.

Redrew Europe after Napoleon: a German Confederation of 39 states, a united Netherlands, Russian Poland, Austria back in northern Italy; it also condemned the Atlantic slave trade (February 1815). It declared Napoleon an outlaw on 13 March 1815.

Napoleon's prison home on a damp plateau of the remote Atlantic island, under close British guard; he dictated his memoirs here and died on 5 May 1821, aged 51.

Tolstoy wrote his novel of Russian society in the years 1805–1812, ending with the burning of Moscow and the retreat, on his estate south of Moscow; it was published 1865–1869.

A ditch dug around Medina defeats a month-long siege by a tribal confederation
Arab victory that ends Byzantine rule in Syria
Arab victory that opens Iraq and the Sasanian capital Ctesiphon
The 'victory of victories' that breaks Sasanian resistance on the Iranian plateau
Tariq ibn Ziyad defeats King Roderic, who is killed; the Visigothic kingdom collapses
Charles Martel defeats Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, who is killed; its long-term importance is debated
The Abbasids defeat a Tang army near the Talas River after its Karluk allies defect
Alp Arslan captures Emperor Romanos IV; Turks then settle across Anatolia
Saladin destroys the crusader army and retakes Jerusalem in October 1187
The Mongols sack Baghdad and kill the last Abbasid caliph of Baghdad
The Mamluks of Egypt halt the Mongol advance into Syria and Egypt
Inconclusive, but Serbia soon becomes an Ottoman vassal
Mehmed II takes Constantinople after a 53-day siege; the Byzantine Empire ends
Ottoman guns defeat Shah Ismail; the Sunni Ottoman - Shia Safavid frontier hardens
Babur's guns defeat Ibrahim Lodi; the Mughal Empire begins
Suleiman defeats Hungary; King Louis II dies; most of Hungary falls to the Ottomans by 1541
Jan Sobieski's relief army breaks the siege; the Ottomans begin to lose Hungary
An artillery duel in the rain turned back the Prussian invasion; the Republic was proclaimed the next day.
Dumouriez's victory opened the Austrian Netherlands (Belgium) to French conquest.
Defeat drove the French out of Belgium; their general Dumouriez defected to the Austrians soon after.
Britain, Spain, Naples, Sardinia, French royalists
The Republic retook the port; the young artillery officer Napoleon Bonaparte made his name in the siege.
Houchard relieved Dunkirk from the Duke of York's siege; he was still guillotined for failing to follow up.
Jourdan and Carnot forced the Austrians to lift the siege of Maubeuge.
Hoche's attack on the Prussians in the Palatinate failed.
The last stand of the Vendéen army after its march north of the Loire; most prisoners were executed.
Howe's fleet (25 ships of the line) took six French ships, but the grain convoy the French were guarding reached France (outcome debated).
Jourdan's victory, watched from a reconnaissance balloon, gave France Belgium for 20 years.
A British-landed émigré army was trapped on the Quiberon peninsula by Hoche; about 750 captured émigrés, including their leader Sombreuil, were shot at Auray.
Bonaparte stormed the Adda bridge; Milan fell five days later.
Archduke Charles defeated Jourdan and drove the French back across the Rhine.
Three days of fighting in the marshes east of Verona; Bonaparte's charge on the bridge became a legend.
The decisive victory of the Italian campaign; Mantua surrendered two weeks later.
Four Austrian relief armies failed; the fortress fell, with about 16,000 Austrian dead or sick and 16,000 captured.
Jervis's 15 ships of the line beat a Spanish fleet of 25 and took four; Nelson won fame here.
Duncan's fleet captured nine Dutch ships of the line, ending the Batavian navy as a threat.
French invasion of Egypt and Syria
French infantry squares broke the Mamluk cavalry; Bonaparte entered Cairo three days later.
French invasion of Egypt and Syria
Nelson destroyed the French fleet in Aboukir Bay (11 of 13 ships of the line taken or destroyed), stranding the army in Egypt.
French invasion of Egypt and Syria
Bonaparte's army, hit by plague, failed to take the fortress and retreated to Egypt.
French invasion of Egypt and Syria
Bonaparte destroyed an Ottoman landing force, then sailed secretly for France a month later.
Suvorov's victory, in which the French commander Joubert was killed, completed the loss of Italy.
Brune defeated the Anglo-Russian invasion of North Holland.
Masséna's victory forced the Russians out of Switzerland and the war.
Nearly lost by midday, won in the evening when Desaix's division arrived (Desaix was killed); it secured Bonaparte's hold on power. Losses: French 5,600–7,000, Austrian 9,402 (modern figure).
Moreau's victory in the snowy forests east of Munich forced Austria into the Peace of Lunéville (February 1801). Austro-Bavarian losses 13,550–15,500, most of them captured.
About 1,200 defenders held a fort against 15,000 French for three weeks, then broke out; a costly French success that showed the expedition would not be easy.
Dessalines' army stormed the last French defences of Cap-Français; Rochambeau surrendered and the French evacuated Saint-Domingue. Haiti declared independence six weeks later.
After a march from the Channel coast, the Grande Armée encircled Mack's army; about 27,000 Austrians surrendered at Ulm itself, with almost no fighting.

Nelson's 27 ships of the line against 33 Franco-Spanish: 18 enemy ships taken or destroyed, Nelson killed. Britain ruled the seas for the rest of the war. Losses: British 458 killed, 1,208 wounded; Franco-Spanish 4,395 killed, 2,541 wounded, about 7,000 captured.

The 'Battle of the Three Emperors': Napoleon lured the allies off the Pratzen heights and broke their centre. Strengths are debated (French 65,000–75,000, allies 73,000–89,000). Austria made peace at Pressburg.
Two battles on one day: Napoleon beat Hohenlohe at Jena while Davout, outnumbered more than two to one, beat the main Prussian army at Auerstedt. Prussia collapsed within weeks.
A bloody draw in a snowstorm in East Prussia. Losses are debated: French 15,000–29,600, Russian 15,000–26,000 (lower figures given here).
Bennigsen's army, trapped with a river at its back, was crushed; Russian losses 20,000–40,000. Tsar Alexander made peace at Tilsit three weeks later.
Fearing Napoleon would seize the neutral Danish fleet, Britain bombarded Copenhagen (2–5 September) and took the whole fleet; hundreds of civilians died. Denmark then sided with France.
Dupont's corps surrendered to Castaños' Spanish army: about 17,000 captured. The first defeat of a Napoleonic army in the open field, it inspired resistance across Europe.
Wellesley (later Wellington) beat Junot north of Lisbon; the Convention of Cintra then let the French leave Portugal on British ships, to public outrage in Britain.
At the end of a winter retreat across Galicia, Moore's army held off Soult so the fleet could take it off; Moore was killed. Tactical British success, strategic French gain (outcome debated).
Napoleon's first personal defeat in a decade: Archduke Charles threw his army back across the Danube near Vienna. Marshal Lannes was mortally wounded.
One of the largest battles fought until then, on the Marchfeld north-east of Vienna; Austria agreed an armistice at Znaim and the Treaty of Schönbrunn.
Wellesley and Cuesta held off Joseph Bonaparte's army west of Madrid, then had to retreat into Portugal; the outcome is disputed, but it made Wellesley Viscount Wellington.
Masséna's assaults on the Bussaco ridge failed; Wellington then fell back to the fortified Lines of Torres Vedras, where the French starved over the winter. Strengths differ widely between sources.
Wellington's attack on Marmont's over-extended army - 'beat 40,000 men in 40 minutes' - opened Madrid to the allies for a few months. French losses 12,000–17,000 including 7,000 captured.

The bloodiest single day of the Napoleonic Wars, 110 km west of Moscow. Kutuzov withdrew and Napoleon entered Moscow, but the Russian army survived. Losses debated: French 30,000–42,000, Russian 40,000–53,000.
The town changed hands many times; afterwards Napoleon gave up the southern road and retreated along the devastated route he had come by.

Pontonniers working in icy water built two bridges at Studianka; about 36,000 effectives escaped, but tens of thousands of stragglers were killed or captured. French loss 50,000–60,000 incl. about 30,000 non-combatants.
Napoleon's new army of young conscripts beat the Russo-Prussian army south of Leipzig, but with too little cavalry to pursue. Strengths and losses vary widely between sources.
Another costly victory without a decisive pursuit; it led to the summer armistice of 1813, during which Austria joined the coalition.
Wellington routed Joseph Bonaparte's army and captured its baggage train, including 151 guns and the king's treasure; French rule in Spain collapsed.
Napoleon's last great victory in Germany, in heavy rain; about 25,000 allied soldiers were captured.

The 'Battle of the Nations', the largest battle in Europe before the First World War, with more than half a million men. Saxon and Württemberg troops changed sides. Losses: coalition 54,000–80,000, French 60,000–79,000.
The first defeat of Napoleon on French soil, in snow near Brienne where he had gone to military school. Strengths vary (78,000–123,000 against 36,000–50,000).
Allied armies stormed Montmartre and Belleville; Paris capitulated and Tsar Alexander rode in on 31 March. Napoleon abdicated at Fontainebleau on 6 April.
Napoleon's last victory: Blücher's Prussians were beaten but retreated north towards Wavre, not east, and so could still reach Waterloo. A further 8,000 Prussians deserted.
Ney failed to take the crossroads from Wellington's army, which could then withdraw to Mont-Saint-Jean.
Britain, Netherlands, Hanover, Nassau, Brunswick, Prussia

Wellington's army held the ridge of Mont-Saint-Jean until Blücher's Prussians arrived on the French flank in the afternoon; the Imperial Guard's last attack failed and the French army broke. Napoleon abdicated four days later.
Four EIC ships beat a larger Portuguese squadron off Surat, winning Mughal favour for an English factory
After fireships scatter the Armada off Calais, the English fleet mauls it at Gravelines (losses: English 50-100 dead and ~400 wounded; Spanish 600+ dead, 800 wounded)
A Dutch fleet breaks into the Medway, burns ships at Chatham and tows away the flagship Royal Charles (Dutch 50-150 casualties, English about 500)
Clive's small army wins after Mir Jafar's troops stand aside; Bengal becomes a company puppet state
Battle of the Plains of Abraham
Wolfe's army climbs to the plateau above Quebec and defeats Montcalm; both generals are killed
Battle of the Plains of Abraham
Hawke chases the French fleet into a rocky bay in a gale (24 v 21 ships of the line) and ends French invasion plans
Hector Munro beats the allied Indian rulers; leads to the diwani of Bengal (1765)
Cornwallis's army surrenders (about 7,500 captured), deciding the war in America
Rodney's 36 ships of the line defeat de Grasse and save Jamaica from invasion (French: ~3,000 killed or wounded, 5,000+ captured)
The fortress is stormed and Tipu Sultan killed; Mysore becomes a subsidiary state (Mysorean losses 6,000-10,000)
Nelson's 27 ships of the line take or destroy 18 of 33; Nelson is killed. British naval supremacy for a century
Last great battle of sailing ships: the allied fleet destroys the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet, securing Greek independence
British ships and the EIC steamer Nemesis take the Bocca Tigris forts and destroy 11 war junks
Storm of Zhenjiang on the Grand Canal; many Manchu defenders killed their families rather than surrender. China sues for peace
Decisive defeat of the Sikh army on the Sutlej (Sikh losses 5,000-8,000)
British and loyal Indian troops storm Delhi; looting and mass killings of civilians follow; Bahadur Shah Zafar exiled
The Residency holds out for 87 days until relief, and is evacuated after a second relief in November
A Zulu army destroys a British column, the worst British defeat against an African army; Zululand is still conquered by July
Boer riflemen drive the British off the hill; Britain restores Transvaal self-rule
A night march and dawn attack crush Urabi's army; Britain occupies Egypt
Kitchener's Maxim guns and rifles kill about 12,000 Mahdists (13,000 wounded) for 47 British-Egyptian dead

Russian battleships took Hull steam trawlers fishing on the Dogger Bank for Japanese torpedo boats and fired on them for ten to twenty minutes: the trawler Crane sank, two fishermen were killed, six wounded and a third man died in May 1905; Russian shells also hit the cruisers Aurora and Dmitry Donskoy, killing a chaplain and a sailor. Position approximate.

Tōgō's Combined Fleet destroyed the Second and Third Pacific Squadrons: all 11 Russian battleships sunk or captured, 21 ships sunk in all. Losses (Wikipedia infobox): Japan 117 dead and 583 wounded, three torpedo boats; Russia 5,045 dead, 803 wounded and 6,016 captured (other counts: 4,380–4,830 killed, 5,917 captured). Crew totals are not given.

campaigns.what: The Chinese monk Faxian walked from Chang'an across the Taklamakan and the Pamirs to India in search of monastic rules, studied at Pataliputra, sailed from Tamralipti to Sri Lanka, and returned by sea via Java or Borneo (the stop is debated), landing in Shandong in 412. Points after Khotan are approximate.

Born in Kucha in 344, Kumarajiva studied in Kashmir (Jibin) and Kashgar as a boy. When the general Lu Guang took Kucha in 384 he was carried off to Guzang (Wuwei) and held there for 17 years, until the Later Qin brought him to Chang'an in 401 to head a translation bureau. Childhood dates are approximate.

Xuanzang left Chang'an in 629 against an imperial ban, crossed the Gobi to Turfan, went round the Tian Shan via Suyab, Tashkent and Samarkand, and over the Hindu Kush by Balkh and Bamiyan to Kashmir and the Ganges plain. After about five years at Nalanda and the assembly at Kannauj in 643 he returned by the southern Silk Road, reaching Chang'an early in 645 with 657 texts. Dates between stops are approximate.

Yijing sailed from Guangzhou on a Persian ship in 671, learned Sanskrit in Srivijaya, and studied at Nalanda for about ten years. He then spent years copying and translating texts in Srivijaya, made a brief trip to Guangzhou in 689 for helpers and paper, and was welcomed at Luoyang by Empress Wu in 695. Intermediate dates are approximate.

Invited in 742 by Japanese monks to bring proper ordination to Japan, the Yangzhou master Jianzhen failed five times; in 748 a storm drove him to Hainan, and on the way back he went blind. His sixth attempt in late 753 succeeded via Okinawa and Kyushu; in Nara he ordained the retired emperor and founded Toshodai-ji in 759. Intermediate dates are approximate.
Muhammad and Abu Bakr hide three days in the cave of Thawr, then travel by a little-used coastal route to Quba and Medina (September 622); exact route approximate.
From Medina through Syria, Egypt and North Africa to Spain in eighty years; Tariq crossed to Spain with about 7,000 men (later reinforced). Dates approximate where the sources differ.
Al-Qadisiyyah, Ctesiphon, Jalula and Nahavand broke the Sasanian Empire; its last king, Yazdegerd III, was killed near Merv in 651. Strengths are rough estimates.
From Shiraz through Makran to Debal, Nerun, Sehwan, Brahmanabad, Alor and Multan; Raja Dahir was killed in 712. Starting force about 6,000 Syrian cavalry; points and dates approximate.

Mansa Musa reached Cairo in July 1324 with an enormous entourage, including many thousands of enslaved people (numbers in later accounts vary widely), and spent so much gold that its value fell; the outward and return routes are approximate (return via Gao and Timbuktu per tradition).

campaigns.who: Louis XVI and the royal family
campaigns.what: The royal family fled the Tuileries in disguise towards the fortress of Montmédy, was recognised at Sainte-Menehould and stopped at Varennes, then brought back to a silent Paris on 25 June. Intermediate times are approximate.

campaigns.who: Prussian, Austrian, Hessian and émigré army
campaigns.what: The Duke of Brunswick's army marched on Paris, took Longwy and Verdun, was halted at Valmy and retreated in rain and dysentery. Dates of intermediate points are approximate.
From Nice to within 150 km of Vienna: Bonaparte knocked Sardinia out of the war, took Lombardy, beat four Austrian relief armies around Mantua and forced Austria to the peace preliminaries of Leoben.
campaigns.w: Italian campaigns of the French Revolutionary Wars

campaigns.what: Bonaparte's fleet left Toulon with about 36,000 soldiers and 167 scholars, seized Malta from the Knights of St John, landed at Alexandria and took Cairo; Nelson destroyed the fleet at Aboukir on 1 August. Sea points between ports are approximate.
campaigns.w: French invasion of Egypt and Syria

campaigns.what: The army gathered at Boulogne to invade England turned east in late August 1805, crossed the Rhine, encircled Mack at Ulm, took Vienna on 13 November and beat the Russians and Austrians at Austerlitz. Dates of intermediate points are approximate.

campaigns.n: Jena campaign and the road to Berlin and Warsaw (1806)
campaigns.what: From Würzburg through the Thuringian Forest to Jena, then north to Potsdam and Berlin (entered 27 October) and on into Prussian Poland, where Napoleon reached Warsaw on 19 December. Intermediate dates approximate.

After Bailén Napoleon came to Spain himself with about 200,000 men (estimate), forced the pass of Somosierra and retook Madrid on 4 December, then marched over the snowbound Guadarrama after Moore's army and turned back at Astorga, leaving the pursuit to Soult.

campaigns.who: British army under Sir John Moore
campaigns.what: Moore advanced from Salamanca against Soult, then turned back when Napoleon came after him: a winter retreat over the Galician mountains with drunkenness, plundering and thousands of stragglers, ending in the battle and evacuation at Corunna. Dates approximate.

Austria attacked Bavaria in April; Napoleon won a string of battles around Regensburg (Abensberg, Landshut, Eckmühl), took Vienna, was repulsed at Aspern-Essling, crossed the Danube again from Lobau island and won at Wagram. Armistice at Znaim on 12 July.

422,000 men crossed the Niemen at Kovno with Napoleon; the main column shrank to about 100,000 by Moscow, mostly through heat, hunger, desertion, typhus and dysentery rather than battle. The drop at Vilnius is mostly detachments (22,000 north towards Riga, 60,000 to Polotsk). Strengths are Minard's figures (his 1869 'Carte figurative', drawn mainly from Fezensac, Labaume and Chambray) for the main column, as digitised by Friendly; they are debated - Riehn counts 685,000 men entering Russia in all and fewer than 70,000 known survivors.

The retreat by the devastated Smolensk road; frost set in from early November (Minard records down to −30 °Réaumur, about −38 °C, in December). The rise to 50,000 at the Berezina is the 30,000 men of the Polotsk corps joining. Only 4,000 of the main column reached the Niemen; with 6,000 of the northern wing, 10,000 recrossed it. Strengths are Minard's figures (his 1869 'Carte figurative', drawn mainly from Fezensac, Labaume and Chambray) for the main column, as digitised by Friendly; they are debated - Riehn counts 685,000 men entering Russia in all and fewer than 70,000 known survivors.

After saying farewell to the Old Guard at Fontainebleau on 20 April, Napoleon travelled south - in disguise for part of the way, as crowds in Provence were hostile - and sailed from Saint-Raphaël on the British frigate Undaunted to Elba, which the Treaty of Fontainebleau gave him as a sovereign principality. Intermediate dates approximate.

campaigns.who: Napoleon and the Armée du Nord
campaigns.what: Napoleon slipped away from Elba with about 1,000 men, landed at Golfe-Juan on 1 March and took the mountain road (today's Route Napoléon) via Digne and Gap; at Laffrey the troops sent to stop him went over to him. He was in the Tuileries on 20 March, invaded Belgium in June and was beaten at Waterloo.

Napoleon surrendered to HMS Bellerophon off Rochefort on 15 July, was kept off Torbay and Plymouth while crowds rowed out to see him, then transferred on 7 August to HMS Northumberland, which reached Jamestown on 15 October. He moved into Longwood House on 10 December. The line is schematic (the ship's course is not drawn).

Second circumnavigation of the world (after Magellan-Elcano): five ships and about 164 men left Plymouth; only the Golden Hind returned, laden with Spanish silver from raids along the Pacific coast (dates of some stops approximate)

141 ships with 10,138 sailors and 19,315 soldiers left Lisbon to escort Parma's army from Flanders; beaten in the Channel, the fleet fled around Scotland and Ireland, where storms wrecked dozens of ships. About 44 ships were lost; the number of men who died is uncertain but ran to many thousands (late dates approximate)

A squadron sent to raid Spain's Pacific empire: scurvy and storms killed most of the 1,854 men and only the Centurion came home, after capturing the Manila galleon Covadonga with 1,313,843 pieces of eight - 188 of the original men survived (dates of some stops approximate)
campaigns.w: George Anson's voyage around the world

campaigns.what: Cook circled the far south, crossing the Antarctic Circle and reaching 71°10'S without finding the supposed great southern continent; his ships avoided serious scurvy thanks partly to diet and hygiene (approximate positions)
Eleven ships carried about 1,420 identified people, more than half of them convicts, 24,000 km in over 250 days to found the penal colony of New South Wales

Schematic 18-month trade voyage of a company ship: woollens, metals and silver out, Indian cotton cloth, tea, silk and porcelain home, sailing with the monsoons via Madras and Whampoa (Canton); dates are typical, not one dated voyage

campaigns.n: Voyage of the Second Pacific Squadron (Libau to Tsushima)
campaigns.what: Rozhestvensky's main force: the new Borodino-class battleships with Oslyabya, cruisers and transports, about 18,000 nautical miles in seven months round Africa, coaling from German colliers off ports that would not admit it. Crew strength along the way is not given in the sources (men left null); points marked approximate in the build notes are interpolated at sea.

The older battleships Sissoi Veliky and Navarin with light cruisers, destroyers and transports took the short way: Tangier, Suda Bay (Crete), the Suez Canal and Djibouti to Nosy Be, arriving 28 December 1904. Dates between Suda Bay and Nosy Be are approximate.

One old battleship (Imperator Nikolai I), three coastal-defence ships and the old cruiser Vladimir Monomakh, sent after Rozhestvensky in February 1905 through the Suez Canal; left Djibouti on 7 April and joined him off French Indochina on 9 May. His staff called them the 'self-sinkers'. Dates between Libau and Djibouti are approximate.

routes.d: The East India Company's long haul around the Cape of Good Hope, using the wide Atlantic loop and the monsoons, until the company was dissolved in 1874
Tea from Canton via the Sunda Strait and St Helena; by 1800 tea made up most of the EIC's China cargo and the clipper 'tea races' ended once steamers used Suez
Bengal opium (an EIC monopoly from 1773) sold at Calcutta to private 'country traders' and smuggled into China via Lintin; legalised in 1858, ended by agreement in 1917

routes.n: Liverpool-New York packet and emigrant route
routes.d: From the Black Ball Line's first scheduled sailing (1818) to the Cunard and White Star steamers, the main road for millions of British, Irish and European emigrants

routes.n: P&O overland mail route to India
routes.d: P&O steamers to Alexandria, overland by Nile boat and carriage to Suez, then steamers via Aden and Galle to India (overland section across Egypt)
After the Suez Canal opened on 17 November 1869 the sea road to India was about 40% shorter; it became the empire's 'lifeline' until the 1956 Suez crisis

routes.n: Coaling stations chain to the Far East
routes.d: British-held coaling ports at Gibraltar, Malta, Port Said, Aden, Colombo, Singapore and Hong Kong let steamships and warships cross half the world under the British flag
